entities.name: Exertional heat stroke
observations: Construction-worker exertion with core temperature 40.6°C and severe central nervous system dysfunction is the classic clinical pattern.
Diaphoresis does not exclude exertional heat stroke; sweating may be preserved early.

entities.name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
observations: Haloperidol exposure makes NMS a leading competing diagnosis; typical supporting findings include hyperthermia, altered consciousness, autonomic instability, rigidity, elevated CK, rhabdomyolysis, and renal injury.

NMS becomes more likely after recent initiation, dose increase, restart, or parenteral administration, especially with generalized lead-pipe rigidity; exertional heat exposure and abrupt workplace collapse favor heat stroke.

entities.name: Malignant hyperthermia
observations: Unlikely without recent volatile anesthetic or succinylcholine exposure; typical clues include rapid rigidity, hypercapnia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, and rhabdomyolysis.

entities.name: Anticholinergic toxicity
observations: Less likely with prominent diaphoresis; anticholinergic toxicity classically causes dry skin, mydriasis, urinary retention, ileus, delirium, and tachycardia.

entities.name: Serotonin toxicity
observations: Requires serotonergic exposure and is suggested by clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, and rapid onset rather than lead-pipe rigidity.

entities.name: Central nervous system infection
observations: Less favored by the occupational heat/exertion context; infectious clues would include meningismus, rash, focal signs, or CSF abnormalities.

entities.name: Status epilepticus
observations: Seizure history warrants EEG consideration, but status epilepticus requires ongoing or recurrent seizure activity or EEG evidence and does not explain the heat/exertion exposure as well.
